## Cardiovascular Outcome Registries and Research (CORR)

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
### 1997 CORR

-   SAS shop
-   Goal: any analyst can pick up any job
-   Folder structure with file naming conventions
-   A social contract — loosely enforced
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### Today

-   R and SAS hybrid
-   Team grows to 19 (and more)
-   Conventions extended to R
-   [Discipline doesn't scale under production pressure]{style="color: #006B5E; font-weight: bold;"}
:::
:::::

::: notes
I work in Cardiovascular Outcomes Registries and Research. CORR was started in 1997, with the arrival of our director Dr. Eugene Blackstone. It started as a pure SAS, small team, social contract held by discipline. R entered not by policy but because the science required it. The hazard SAS/C procedure, randomForestSRC, and ggRandomForests methods were created to solve the science questions. The goal is to use the best methodology to answer the questions.
:::

. . .

SAS/C PROC `hazard` for survival analysis (1986).

R package `randomForestSRC` survival, regression, classification (2007).

R package `ggRandomForests` RFSRC graphics (2012).

**Nobody planned a hybrid shop. The science pulled R in.**

We are concerned with the scale that this social contract has to support. 19 staff driving 150 data requests, 100+ presentations, and 50 manuscripts a year — all feeding 1,100+ HVTI publications. Every inefficiency in the pipeline multiplies across all of that. This is what "operating at scale" means here. 
:::

::: notes
That 19 staff are split between disciplines. Data managers/Engineers focus primarily on getting data from medical systems to our warehouse, stat programmers assemble the data into analysis data sets, biostatisticans build an analysis report that researchers convert into manuscripts and presentations. Data flows through systems; people transform it at each step. The biostatistician sits at the core — taking a clean analysis dataset and producing an Analysis Report that researchers can build a manuscript from. Since this is an audience of R users, we can focus on the that component of the pipeline.
:::

::: notes
The biostatistician produces the Analysis Report, the product we deliver. Jobs are the implementation detail — what the audience cares about is the report that comes out the other side. The three-column structure here maps directly onto the talk: data ingestion produces a clean dataset, model building produces estimates, results and figures produce a report. Scaling the team means making every step of that pipeline reliable and handoff-ready.
:::

## Reproducibility at scale — Three Focus Areas {background-color="#006B5E"}

::: {style="font-size: 1.8em; line-height: 1.8;"}
1. Data ingestion
2. Model building
3. Figures and tables
:::

::: notes
These are the three places where reproducibility breaks down in practice. Each section follows the same structure: here's what it looked like before, here's the failure mode, here's what we're doing about it. The solutions are at different stages — some in production, some rolling out, some still aspirational.
:::

::: notes
The folder structure isn't the problem — it works. Dataset filenaming MIGHT work. The problem is what happens inside datasets/ when an extract gets updated. Naming and modified dates weren't designed for this job.
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 1.4em; margin-top: 0.5em;"}
*Is this the right data? Has it changed?*
:::

## How we're addressing it [In development]{.badge-dev}

**Layer governance on top of existing structure.**

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
### What we have

::: {style="font-size: 1.7em;"}
```
study_root/
  analyses/      ← jobs
  datasets/      ← *this problem*
  descriptive/
  distributions/
  documents/     ← office docs
  estimates/     ← cached data
  graphs/        ← pdf graphics
```
:::

File naming convention for datasets: `built.sas7bdat`
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### What we're adding

-   Date in the filename; never overwrite
-   Dataset manifest — source, date, extract parameters
-   Checksum — detect silent changes
-   Audit trail — job ↔ manifest
:::
:::::

::: notes
The folder structure is already there and it works. Over the past 25 years, we've created 1400 studies. Jobs in analysis... read datasets, stored models and results in estimates, graphs. This problem resides inside datasets/ — we need a way to know whether the file the analysis ran against is the same file that's there now. Manifests and checksums do that without changing the structure anyone is used to.
:::

## Manifest + checksum in practice [In development]{.badge-dev}

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
**`datasets/built260430.manifest.yml`**

```yaml
dataset:      built260430.sas7bdat
source:       Cardiopulse / STS registry v2.1
pulled_by:    data_manager
pull_date:    2026-04-30
sha256:       a3f8c2d1e4b7f093...
observations: 12847
variables:    428
```
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
**Register explicitly — separate from build**

```r
digest::digest(
  "datasets/built260430.sas7bdat",
  algo = "sha256", file = TRUE)
```

**Verify before analysis**

```r
stored  <- yaml::read_yaml(
  "datasets/built260430.manifest.yml")$sha256
current <- digest::digest(
  "datasets/built260430.sas7bdat",
  algo = "sha256", file = TRUE)
stopifnot(current == stored)
```

[Filename says *when*. Checksum says *whether*.]{.muted}
:::

:::::

::: notes
The checksum is stored at registration — a deliberate step separate from file creation. If the file is rebuilt (extract re-run, data corrected), the old checksum stays in the manifest and jobs will fail until someone consciously re-registers. This makes rebuilds loud by default. The date-stamped filename tells you when the extract was pulled; the checksum tells you whether the file you're reading now is the same one that was registered. Doesn't tell you a new dataset exists — only that the registered one hasn't changed.

We now have the path to do this in R, and need to extend to SAS.
:::

. . .

Rebuild without re-registering → every downstream job fails.
**That failure is the feature.**

# Model Building {background-color="#34495e"}

::: notes
:::

## Problem: R and SAS Environments

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**SAS**

-   SAS version not locked to a study
-   Shared Macro library unversioned
-   Shared server
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**R & RStudio**

-   R version is not locked to a study
-   Shared Package library — package versions drift
-   Shared server 
-   Serialized models in `estimates/` **fail to load**
-   Results don't match — or the job won't run
:::
:::::

::: notes
Neither platform captures the environment. SAS's shared server setup makes it invisible; RStudio helps with Projects, if we use them. R's global package library makes it fragile. The failure modes look different but the root cause is the same: no one pinned the environment to the study.
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 1.4em; margin-top: 0.5em;"}
*Can you reproduce this analysis six months from now?*
:::

## R: `renv` with RStudio projects [In use]{.badge-inuse}

```{=html}
<style>
.renv-split { display: grid; grid-template-columns: 1fr 44px 1fr; gap: 0; }
.renv-bad { background: #fdf2f2; border: 2px solid #e74c3c; border-radius: 8px 0 0 8px; padding: 12px 16px; display: flex; flex-direction: column; }
.renv-good { background: #f0faf5; border: 2px solid #006B5E; border-radius: 0 8px 8px 0; padding: 12px 16px; display: flex; flex-direction: column; }
.renv-arr { display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: center; font-size: 1.8em; color: #aaa; background: #f4f4f4; }
.renv-head { font-size: 0.78em; font-weight: 700; margin-bottom: 8px; text-transform: uppercase; letter-spacing: 0.05em; padding-bottom: 5px; border-bottom: 2px solid currentColor; }
.renv-bad .renv-head { color: #c0392b; }
.renv-good .renv-head { color: #006B5E; }
.renv-item { font-size: 0.72em; padding: 4px 0; border-bottom: 1px solid rgba(0,0,0,0.07); line-height: 1.4; color: #333; }
.renv-step { font-size: 0.74em; font-weight: 700; color: #006B5E; margin-top: 7px; margin-bottom: 2px; }
.renv-step-sub { font-size: 0.62em; color: #888; margin-bottom: 3px; }
.renv-code { background: #1e1e1e; color: #ccc; border-radius: 4px; padding: 6px 10px; font-family: 'Courier New', monospace; font-size: 0.6em; line-height: 1.7; }
.renv-lock { background: #006B5E; color: #fff; border-radius: 6px; padding: 5px 10px; text-align: center; font-size: 0.6em; font-weight: 700; line-height: 1.6; margin: 5px auto; display: block; width: fit-content; }
.renv-ok { font-size: 0.74em; color: #006B5E; font-weight: 600; margin-top: 5px; line-height: 1.5; }
</style>

<div class="renv-split">
  <div class="renv-bad">
    <div class="renv-head">Without renv</div>
    <div class="renv-item">Packages installed globally &mdash; shared across all projects</div>
    <div class="renv-item"><code>update.packages()</code> breaks other analyses silently</div>
    <div class="renv-item">Serialized models in <code>estimates/</code> fail to load 6 months later</div>
    <div class="renv-item">&ldquo;Works on my machine&rdquo; &mdash; but not yours</div>
    <div class="renv-item">New analyst hunts down exact versions to reproduce results</div>
  </div>
  <div class="renv-arr">&rarr;</div>
  <div class="renv-good">
    <div class="renv-head">With renv</div>
    <div class="renv-step">Day 1 &mdash; any analyst, any machine</div>
    <div class="renv-step-sub">Isolate the project library and freeze it</div>
    <div class="renv-code">
      <span style="color:#569cd6;">renv</span>::init()&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<span style="color:#6a9955;"># isolate library</span><br>
      <span style="color:#569cd6;">renv</span>::install(<span style="color:#ce9178;">"ehrlinger/hvtiPlotR"</span>)<br>
      <span style="color:#569cd6;">renv</span>::snapshot()&nbsp;&nbsp;<span style="color:#6a9955;"># freeze versions</span>
    </div>
    <div class="renv-lock">renv.lock &mdash; R 4.4.1 &middot; hvtiPlotR 0.3.2 &middot; &hellip;<br><span style="font-weight:400;">commit this; it travels with the project</span></div>
    <div class="renv-step">6 months later &mdash; different analyst, different machine</div>
    <div class="renv-step-sub">Open .Rproj, run one command</div>
    <div class="renv-code">
      <span style="color:#569cd6;">renv</span>::restore()&nbsp;&nbsp;<span style="color:#6a9955;"># rebuilds library from renv.lock</span>
    </div>
    <div class="renv-ok">Same packages. Same results. The job belongs to the team.</div>
  </div>
</div>
```

::: notes
The key word is "handoff." renv makes the job transferable, not just reproducible on your own machine. The lockfile travels with the project; the library itself gets rebuilt locally on renv::restore(). SAS has no equivalent — that's an open problem we note in the status table.
:::

## Problem: Shared function libraries aren't versioned

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**SAS macro library**

-   Centralized — everyone calls the same macros
-   Not versioned — no record of which version ran
-   Changes propagate silently
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**R functions**

-   Copied at study creation — diverges immediately
-   Fixes stay local; no propagation
-   In-flight studies never get updates
:::
:::::

::: notes
Two different failure modes, equally bad. SAS centralizes but can't control when changes land — every study gets every update whether ready or not. R isolates studies from each other but also from improvements — fixes stay local and diverge over time. Neither platform has a deliberate, versioned release process.
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 1.4em; margin-top: 0.5em;"}
*SAS: did that update break something? R: did anyone else get that fix?*
:::

## R: internal packages (SAS macros) [In development]{.badge-dev}

A package **is** a versioned, distributable library.

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Functions in a study folder**

- Frozen at copy
- Fixes don't propagate
- No version record
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Code in a package**

- One canonical version
- Pull fixes deliberately with `renv::update()`
- Examples double as tests
:::
:::::

::: notes
Packages are better than scattered copies, but the governance problems shift rather than disappear. The version choice becomes explicit and deliberate — which is exactly the point.
:::

. . .

**The hard problems shift — they don't disappear.**

- Someone must own releases.
- Studies must pin versions deliberately.

## Problem: Code and results live separately

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**SAS — partially solved this**

-   `.lst` pairs code and output
-   Figures still separate files

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**R scripts — no equivalent**

-   Code and output in separate files
-   No standard structure
-   Figures disconnected from code
:::
:::::

::: notes
SAS solved the code+output problem with .lst. R has no equivalent yet. Note: we still have the underlying copy/paste problem — both SAS jobs and R scripts are copied from a central templates folder, meaning in-flight studies don't get updates. Quarto and packages are the foundation we're building first before tackling that propagation problem.
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 1.4em; margin-top: 0.5em;"}
*Can a new analyst navigate this job without asking whoever wrote it?*
:::

## R: Quarto analysis reports [In development]{.badge-dev}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**`report.qmd` = `job.sas`**

-   Code and output in one document
-   Figures inline
-   Renders to HTML, PDF, Word

**Always render before committing.**
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Standard 4-section template**

```markdown
# Data.qmd
Ingestion, exclusions, cohort description

# Methods.qmd
Model specification and assumptions

# Explainability.qmd
Diagnostics, sensitivity checks

# Results.qmd
Tables, figures, interpretation
```

[The structure is the contract.]{.muted}
:::
:::::

::: notes
The pitch to SAS analysts isn't "learn a new tool" — it's "get what you already have in .lst, but with real figures inline and a structure everyone agrees on." The 4-section template is the standard we're building toward: consistent enough to navigate, flexible enough to cover every study type.
:::

# Figures and Tables {background-color="#34495e"}

::: notes
:::

## The Problem: Publication-quality graphics

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**SAS: `plot.sas`**

- Hard-won publication quality
- Each output target: more manual effort

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**R: `ggplot2`**

- Same per-target effort problem
- No shared themes or palettes
:::
:::::

::: notes
The energy never went away — it just moved platforms. plot.sas was hard-won: we bent SAS graphics into publication quality, but every new output target meant more formatting work. ggplot2 is more flexible but the same two problems persist: the per-target formatting effort, and analysts diverging on themes and color palettes. hvtiPlotR addresses both — capturing the effort in a package and enforcing shared standards through the S3 plot. pattern.
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 1.4em; margin-top: 0.5em;"}
*Can we capture that effort once — and ensure every analyst's figures look the same?*
:::

## R: standardized pipeline [In development]{.badge-dev}

**The package does the hard work. The analyst decorates.**

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Package owns**

- The statistical transform
- The base figure — correct by construction
- Themes: manuscript, PowerPoint, poster

**Analyst owns**

- Axis labels, annotations
- Nothing else needs to change
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
# Package handles the figure
fig <- plot(corr_analysis(data))

# Analyst decorates to context
fig +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  annotate("text", ...)
```

*If it looks like the package example, it's correct.*
:::
:::::

::: notes
The S3 pattern matters because it separates concerns cleanly. The transform function does the statistical work and returns a typed object. The plot method knows how to visualize that object. The analyst's job is decoration — choosing scales, adding annotations — not rebuilding the figure from scratch. The package examples are the documentation AND the quality standard: if your figure matches the example, it's correct. This is how we recover the consistency that plot.sas enforced, without locking people into SAS.
:::

## Our visualization packages [In development]{.badge-dev}

**`ggRandomForests`** — [github.com/ehrlinger/ggRandomForests](https://github.com/ehrlinger/ggRandomForests)

Variable importance, partial depth, minimal depth — `ggplot2` objects built around `randomForestSRC`.

<br>

**`hvtiPlotR`** — [github.com/ehrlinger/hvtiPlotR](https://github.com/ehrlinger/hvtiPlotR)

Survival curves, hazard plots, forest plots in CORR themes. Bridges `ggplot2` to `plot.sas` standards.

<br>

*The science keeps moving. So do the packages.*

::: notes
ggRandomForests is the proof of concept — born from an internal need, built as a package, and eventually adopted externally. It was removed from CRAN because of dependency drift, not design failure; the pattern still holds. hvtiPlotR applies the same model to CORR-specific plot types. The honest note here is that these packages are always in development — the science keeps moving, and the package has to keep up. That's a governance problem as much as a technical one.
:::

## The framing shift that mattered {background-color="#34495e"}

::: {style="font-size: 1.8em; line-height: 1.5; margin-bottom: 0.8em;"}
"Reproducibility" → **"Production reliability"**
:::

*"Any biostatistician can pick up any job."*

The tools don't change. The reason to adopt them does.

::: notes
Reproducibility framing failed us — it reads as an academic virtue, something you do for reviewers. Production reliability framing landed differently with the team: it's about whether someone else can pick up your job on a Monday morning when you're out sick. Same tools, same practices — but the reason to adopt them shifted from "good science hygiene" to "your teammates won't be stranded." The second framing wins buy-in. Make the right path the easy path means the standards have to be lower-friction than the workaround, or people will always take the workaround.
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 1.4em; margin-top: 0.5em;"}
**Make the right path the easy path.**
:::

::: notes
This table is the honest answer to "how far along are you?" The folder structure and naming conventions are long-standing and solid — that's the foundation everything else builds on. renv is the easy win we're rolling out now. The packages are in use but actively changing. Everything in Aspirational is real and planned, but not yet standard practice. The point isn't to apologize for the gaps — it's to show that this is a real production environment with real constraints, not a clean academic case study.
:::
